they had made a big mistake and they cack -handedly sought to falsify the Hansard
record.
He said yesterday, on the issue of his awareness of staff involvement, the
following—and I quote him—“of which I was aware,”. Yesterday’s video of Parliament
clearly has him saying that, but in last night’s Hansard, all of a sudden, the word “not”
was put before the word “awar e,” so that in the Hansard last night it reads “of which I
was not aware,”. Yesterday Mr Flavell uttered the truth, before a cover -up that must not
be allowed to succeed. Now the word “not” —you would not believe it —is back out of
the Hansard. What on earth is going on with the leading institution of this country when
it is claimed that the Hansard people put the word “not” in there? Who would do that?
When you saw the video or you heard what was said, there is no way there could
have been a mistake. He tri ed to change the record, but in doing so he more deeply
implicated himself because what he denied before the Māori Affairs Committee on 17
June in the afternoon in Parliament, then this week in Parliament, and again today was
caught out by his Hansard record—now corrected —which reads “of which I was
aware,”. And how can a Minister get by making denial after denial when it was said by
the Prime Minister: “I’m a Prime Minister who believes in standards —high standards.”
Well, these standards are so low you could parachute out of the bottom of a snake and
have room to spare. Over and over it goes on.
I want to say to the National -led Government, and more particularly to the Māori
Party and Māori members over there, that we will never have equality in this count ry if
substandard performance and second -class standards is the benchmark for Māori
politicians. We will never have equality if that is what is accepted by your European
colleagues in the National Government. It is inverse racism of the worst sort. The las t
thing that any Māori wants is this paternalistic treatment that says: “Well, he’s a Māori
Minister; we don’t expect better.”
Well, we in New Zealand First do expect better. We have always opposed Whānau
Ora. The only party in this Parliament that has opposed Whānau Ora because of its
corruption is New Zealand First. But the Minister sought, and his staff sought, to
interfere and break the law and to spike —stop—a debate because he did not want to
face New Zealand First. That is enough for the Minister to go, but the denials over and
over and over again, and the circus we saw in the House today on points of order about
that Hansard change, tell us that he should go. I regret saying that—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: No, you don’t.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I do regret saying that. I know him better than you
do. I know him far better than that member over there does, but I am sick of those
members over there telling me they believe in equality. They are telling me they believe
in one law f or all, but when it comes to standards and performance and accountability,
4718 General Debate 24 Jun 2015
they clearly do not. Again, I say that that Minister, in the interests of Māoridom’s
integrity, let alone that of this country and of this Parliament, should resign.
You know, Mara ma Fox got involved within hours of the programme being shut
down to try to convince Mihi Forbes that the Māori Party was not involved. Why would
she do that?
Do not forget that on 22 June, 2 days after the shutdown, you had the chief executive
officer for Māori Television —namely, this man, Paora Maxwell —saying that content
was discussed. The Minister kept denying it. What is this photograph here about? Well,
this is a photograph of him being taken on to the marae to welcome him as the new
chief executive officer of Māori Television. What is fascinating about that is this: when
this event happened, Te Ururoa Flavell was not the Minister in charge of Māori
Television. He did not get that job until 8 months later. So the question is: are the
allegations true that Māori Party interference in Māori Television was happening a long
way back and that it is happening still? The answer is palpably, demonstrably yes. Mr
Te Ururoa Flavell should be resigning.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I again thank the whips
for giving me another slot for the drive-time audience of Auckland. In fact, I almost feel
I should be like Selena on breakfast TV and have my iPad out and take you through a
traffic forecast for Auckland. But I am not going to do that.
What I am going to do today is give a little lesson to the Labour Party members. It is
a genuine lesson. It is not going to be rude. It is not going to be nasty. I want them to
listen carefully. I am going to throw a bit of mathematics in it. For example, I am going
to talk about monotonic functions. Most people do not know —they think monotone is a
dreary, dull speaker —that a monotonic function is a graph that heads in one direction
and keeps doing it. Here is my lesson. I have gone back and I have looked at the two
main parties, Labour and National, right back into the 1930s, and I have looked at
general elections and what has happened when there has been a change of Government.
We know there is a famous statement here that Oppositions do not win elections;
Governments lose them. In fact, all you need to do—and I suggest to people on the
other side that they get their research people to do it—is to draw these graphs, because it
is just so factual it is not funny. Every time there has been a general election in the past
that changed the Government, from that point on the Government’s support has started
to drop, and the Opposition party started to grow in a monotonic fashion—that is, a
general increase.
So we go back through history. Take 1975, when Rob Muldoon won. By 1978
National had dropped dramatically. By 1981 it just got there by about one seat from the
Springbok tour. Three years after 1981, by 1984, there was a complete and a bsolute
clean-out. Why am I telling the Labour Party members all this? I am telling them this
because what has happened now is that history has somehow changed the political
landscape.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Tell us about 2002. Bill English—22 percent.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: It is no good for Mr Mallard to keep yelling and
screaming about this. He really should listen, because he just needs to look at the
graphs. This is not the National Party’s view. This is not whether the Labour Party
thinks this is a great Government or not. This is what the public think of the
performance of their politicians. Once the John Key -  led Government had won the
election in 2008 what should have happened after that—actually, I hear Mr Mallard say:
“Tell us about 2002.” Actually, Labour dropped in 2002 from what it had got in 1999.
Yes, there was a huge aberration. For the first time in the history of the country an
Opposition party—National—went down in 2002. It is the only time in the history of
the graphs that that has happened.
24 Jun 2015 General Debate 4719
But let us come back to the last 3 years, because this is where it gets interesting. This
is where it gets frightening for the Labour Party. After the 2008 win by the John Key -
led Government, Labour should have expected its poor performance, reflected in 2008,
to start lifting and by 2011 be within sort of striking distance, and certainly by 2014 to
be right knocking on the door and if it does not make it , well, you know, it is a little bit
like the Brash-led party of 2005 when it did not quite make it but on the night you could
not tell. But that is not what has happened—that is not what has happened. My lesson to
the Labour Party today is that you should be very, very afraid of what is going on,
because you are not making any traction in the polls. You can get up and blame this
Government and say that we are useless and we are hopeless and so on. I do not mind
you doing that. But why are the public not re sponding to the Labour Party, as they
normally would in Opposition? Labour members say: “We’re coming back; we’re
coming back.”. They are not. They have got very limited time. Elections are not won in
the last 6 months of the 3- year period. You cannot do i t. The history of it is that unless
you have got yourself well back in the polls, you cannot do it.
My lesson to Labour members is that they need to really scurry around fast and
say—the polling is showing it. Our polling is showing it— I am sure they are doing the
same sort of polling —and the general polls are showing it: Labour is actually lower in
the polls now than it was 3 years ago or 6 years ago. The Labour leader is lower in the
polls than previous other leaders, before Cunliffe and so on. So they have got a limited
time frame. Instead of carping on about what a useless Government we are or how the
National Party is not building enough houses, Labour members should go back to first
principles and say: “What is it we need to do to turn these polls round?”. If they do not,
they are guaranteed a fourth term in Opposition, and right now, the way they are
polling, that is exactly where they are destined.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Referring to the fact that Mr
Williamson said Labour cannot do it, I just want to say: “Watch this space, Mr
Williamson. Watch this space.” We can, and we will, Mr Williamson. Let us see what
happens in 2017. We have listened to a few National Party speeche s today. We had Tim
Macindoe telling us that the Government is sticking to a plan that works —the
Government is sticking to a plan that works. Well, if the plan is to sell out New
Zealand, then it is doing a good job of it. If the plan is to sell out the most vulnerable
New Zealanders, then the Government is doing a good job of it. Mr Macindoe said that
good public services do not necessarily mean expensive public services. Well, actually,
$140,000 for a TV screen at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Mr
Macindoe, is expensive in our minds. At least, Mr Macindoe, on this side of the House
we want to put taxpayers’ money into people, not into $140,000 TV screens, not into
$74,000 reception desks, and not into $1,000 seats for people to sit on. We want to put
our public money into the New Zealand public.
We listened to Scott Simpson saying that Labour likes to talk about “no” —that the
word on this side of the House is “no”. They think that we are “no, no, no” to good
ideas. But let us reflect o n what National has said no to over the 7 years that it has been
Government. When National first got in, it said no to apprenticeships: “We can take
money out of that. We don’t need that.” Then what happened? We had an earthquake,
and we did not have the e xpertise here. The Government had to ship it in. The
Government said no to things like healthy food in our schools. One of the first things
that the Government did was cut the policy of healthy food in our schools, and now we
see the Government struggling with the issue that we have with obesity and our
children. Why did the Government remove that policy? We see the Government saying
no to building houses in Auckland. There is a demand for housing in Auckland, and that
Government says no to new houses.
4720 General Debate 24 Jun 2015
That side of the House has said no to healthy homes. We put up a healthy homes bill,
and the Government said no to it. The Government does not care about the health and
well-being of New Zealanders, even when we have instances like the one we had
recently where a small child died because of the fact that she was living in an unhealthy
home.
The Government said no to extending paid parental leave. The Government said no
to the paid parental leave bill that my colleague Sue Moroney put up.
A few years ago the Government said no to adult community education. It cut all the
funding to adult community education, which for many people was their first step back
into the education system.
The Government said no to the training incentive allowance, not wanting to support
sole parents to be able to increase their earning capacity —to increase their chances of
getting a better-qualified, higher-paying job.
The Government recently said no to KiwiSaver, thereby denying children who enter
into the scheme the $1,000 incentive. The Government says that we are the party of
“no”, but its track record says that it is the party of “no”.
I think the whole country should be concerned about the things that the Government
has said yes to. It has said yes to foreign property speculator s being able to buy our
houses. Here we are with a housing market that it is difficult for New Zealand families
to get into, and the Government still allows non -residents, non-citizens, to come here
and buy our New Zealand houses, thereby driving the price s up and making it
impossible for families to be able to get into their own home. The Government said yes
to experimenting with our most vulnerable New Zealanders. The Government is now
looking at introducing social impact bonds, when there has been no res earch done here
that qualifies or justifies the Government being able to implement them. The
Government said yes to selling out our social services to big multinational corporations.
On Sunday we had the Minister for Social Development on Q+A  confirming that she
would contemplate the idea of selling out our social services to a company like Serco,
which has an international reputation such that no New Zealander would be happy about
handing their social services over to it.
What else has the Government said yes to? It has said yes to the Conservative Party,
despite the fact that the whole board walked out on that party. The Government has said
yes to asset sales. That was not a very good economic strategy. The Government has
said yes to Rio Tinto. The Governm ent has said yes to Nick Smith, even. We have got
all the evidence in the world to suggest that he is not doing a good job. The Government
still says yes, and we have the Prime Minister saying that Nick Smith is outstanding.
We might be saying no to some of what the National Party is suggesting, but we are
justified in saying no to what it is doing. The Government is not justified in what it has
said no to over the past 7 years.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: That speech has definitely proved that it is
that side that is the “no” party. This side believes in yes. It is under this National
Government, under the leadership of the Rt Hon John Key, that our economy is
growing, wages are rising, there are more jobs out there, inflation is negligible, and
interest rates are staying lower for longer. This shows that our plan is working and that
we are sticking to a plan that is working.
This National Government is a very efficient and fair Governme nt. For example, our
tax system is fair to all. We believe in a low -rate tax system that responds to our needs
in a planned manner. We believe in rewarding people for their hard work, not punishing
people for their hard work. We believe in low compliance a nd administrative costs. It is
this National Government that is working hard to minimise tax avoidance and evasion
opportunities. Since 2008 it is this National Government that has given a reduction in
24 Jun 2015 General Debate 4721
the personal tax rate and a reduction in the company t ax rate, and it is this National
Government that has just announced firm rules around property taxes.
This has been possible because we have a plan that is working. We want to keep our
taxes to the minimum, and that is why we rejected Labour’s capital gai ns tax idea. Yes,
we rejected the capital gains tax idea, which was Labour’s idea. This is with the target
of getting our net debt below 20 percent of GDP by 2020—net debt below 20 percent of
GDP by 2020. This is without putting any extra burden on taxpaye rs. Again, this has
been possible because we have a plan that is working.
It is under this National Government that the number of people who are under the
age of 20 and who are not in any employment and who are not in any training or
education is the lowe st since 2004. Yes, the lowest since 2004. Is it not a great
achievement of this National Government? Yes, it is a great achievement of this
National Government. This National Government is working hard to reduce welfare
dependency. We are working hard to uplift skills in our people. We are working hard to
reduce crime, and we are working hard to improve interaction with Government. By
working in these areas, we are getting better outcomes for our people.
When you talk to people, what do they want? They wa nt, firstly, good educations for
their children, and they are getting that under this National Government. They want
jobs. Yes, they are getting jobs, because there are more jobs being created under this
National Government. And the next thing they want is  to be safe, and that is another
great achievement of this National Government, because under this National
Government crime is the lowest since 1978. Yes, and this has been possible because this
National Government is hard on crime. This National Governme nt is hard on criminals.
We have more cops on roads. Yes, we have more cops on roads because we have
provided them with modern- day technology: smartphones and tablets. So instead of
sitting in their offices, they are on roads. Each cop is saving 30 minutes  of their office
time, and that equals 354 additional cops on roads. That equals half a million hours of
cops on roads New Zealand - wide per annum, and that is how we have the lowest crime
since 1978 under this National Government.
Our justice system is focused on the rights of victims. New Zealand families deserve
to feel safe in their homes and communities, and our strategy is working. Our approach
is working. Our plan is working, and that is why, in Budget 2015, $218.6 million was
allocated to do that, and $40 million was allocated to improve services and efficiencies
in targeted areas in justice and courts. By investing in these agencies, we are getting
better outcomes for New Zealand families.
Our money that is allocated for the Serious Fraud Office s hows that we are really
serious about our international reputation, because New Zealand is known as a safe
place to do business and invest. This National Government takes any kind of misuse
very seriously. This National Government has already saved $60 mil lion of taxpayers’
money since we started the national benefit fraud reform initiative over 2 years ago.
Yes, $60 million of taxpayers’ money was saved by this National Government. There
are 9,500 people off benefits, because they were on because of benefi t fraud. They are
off benefits. There are 9,500 people off benefits. Thank you.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker. Thank you for allowing me this opportunity to finish, certainly, the debate
from this side of the House. As I start, I would like to acknowledge Norm Berryman
and his passing, and pay my respects to him. I played club rugby wit h Norm Berryman
in the far north, and he will be sorely missed amongst the people in the north. Our
prayers and our thoughts are with him and his family. Norm Berryman was able to slice
through the middle of some of the best rugby teams in the world. He wa s able to pick
4722 General Debate 24 Jun 2015
out some of the smallest gaps and exploit their weaknesses. You do not need such a
keen eye as Norm Berryman’s to find the weaknesses in this current Government.
What we are seeing from this Government is confusion. The campaign picture of all
rowing in the same direction is but a distant memory. Housing —let us take housing, for
example. We have two Ministers in particular engaging in what seems like an icy cold
stare. That icy cold stare is around the right of first refusal. It seems to me that what this
Government is doing is trampling on the integrity and the so- called good faith that was
entered into with the iwi of Tāmaki -makau-rau in making sure that they have the right
of first refusal on land to allow them to develop it for the well- being of their people.
You do not need to look too far to know that it is probably strategic that Minister Smith
is behind Minister Finlayson, so that they are not able to engage further in that long,
cold, icy stare.
You throw into the mix, into that whol e right of first refusal, the Māori Party —the
Māori Party, which since getting into bed with the National Government has claimed
that “We are at the table; we are able to influence these decisions.” Well, what
happened when the right of first refusal came around? All those members could say
was: “Well, we’ve written a letter to the Prime Minister.” What happened to this solid
relationship that they claim out in our regions? What happened to this “We are getting
the benefits for our people.”? What it showed me is that they, just like anyone on this
side of the House, only have the power to write a letter to the Prime Minister. And what
has been the answer? Silence—exactly.
I want to talk a little bit about poverty, too. Just not long ago, all this Government
talked about was how it was focusing on poverty, how it was pouring all of this money
into identifying what poverty is and how it was going to fix it. Well, at the moment, just
like the previous question I just asked, what is the answer, and what is it doing now?
Nothing. It slipped entirely off the radar. The Government has forgotten about poverty.
It has forgotten about the regions. Why? Because it does not know how to invest in
them. It does not know how to solve these issues.
To some of the more posit ive economic things —tourism. Just before I came down
here, I was in my office with the chief executive of Tourism New Zealand, who was
giving me a great conversation and a great presentation about how well tourism is
doing. So then why, when members of thi s Government attended particular seminars
and conferences with the tourism industry, which clearly said to them: “We do not want
a tax for people who are coming in and out of this country.”—what did this Government
do? It turned its back on that industry. It was a complete surprise, in the Budget
announcement, to the tourism—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: They deceived them.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: They deceived them. It was a complete surprise to the tourism
industry when that announcement was made during the Budget. In fact, I have received
numerous complaints about this Government not listening to the tourism industry. It is
such a valuable industry in this country, and this Government turns its back on it. This
is not a Government with a plan, or a future, or a hope. I have already mentioned the
campaign picture of rowing in one direction. Well, it looks like not everybody is
wearing a blue T-shirt. In this case, they are all rowing the wrong way.
Finally, we talk about the holes and the part y falling apart. If there is one thing that
sticks together in this party —I am reminded of a dag on the rear end of a sheep. We
know just how sticky that can be, and just how unified that can be, but we know just
how important sheep are to this particular Government. A little bit of sand might be able
to help with those dags on the back of a sheep. We hope that this Government actually
wakes up to its own arrogance, but it is a little bit difficult when all you do is talk to
yourselves about all the important matters facing New Zealand.
24 Jun 2015 General Debate 4723
Finally, we here on this side of the House have a positive look for the future. We are
looking with aspiration for the future of New Zealand. Māori Television will see better
days. Housing will see better days. Tēnā koe.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
First Reading
Debate resumed from 3 June.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The last time we were
considering this bill, Jonathan Young w as speaking. He has 1 minute left, if he so
wishes.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant
Speaker. Yes, absolutely, I do want to take up my 1 minute.
I want to acknowledge the honourable member Damien O’Connor, who put this bill
in. Everything in politics is a matter of timing, and perhaps when the bill was lodged in
the ballot the timing was right, but it is not right now because legislation has overtaken
the intent of this bill. The legislation has overtaken the intent of this bill, and, in fact, the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment produced this document in 2013,
which says Safe mines: safe workers —New laws —new laws —on mining health and
safety: A quick guide for mine operators.
Can I just mention a couple of things it says in the introduction? It says: “The
Government has recently made changes to the laws concerning health and safety in the
mining industry. This is in response to the recommendations of the Royal Commission
on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy and will bring New Zealand’s approach to mining
health and safety into line with international best practice.”

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I regret to inform the
member his time has expired.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I want to acknowledge
my colleague the Hon Damien O’Connor for introducing the Underground Coal Mining
Safety Bill as a response to the tragedy that occurred within his own electorate, which
so deeply affected his electorate and which, to this day, still so deeply affects his
electorate. I want to just comment on the final comment made by Jonathan Young there.
He said that timing is everything, and that there once was a time when this bill might
have had a place but that that time has gone and has been overtaken by events and been
overtaken by all the actions tha t the Government has taken. Oh, if only that were the
case. If only the Government actually maintained the focus on health and safety that it
had in the days and weeks after the Pike River disaster.
It was a wake- up call for all of us. Years and years of reliance on the ideological
view that deregulation was the answer to everything led us, ultimately, to that tragedy
occurring. In the days and weeks after it the Prime Minister said and did all the right
things. The Government members said and did all the right things. They knew that they
had no choice. It was politically untenable for the Government not to address health and
safety not only in the mining sector but in all other industries in New Zealand. Our
health and safety record in this country is woef ul. We have twice the rate of death and
injury that they have in the United Kingdom, and in Australia their rate of injury at
work is around just two- thirds what ours is here in New Zealand. We have to act. We
have known that for a long time, but it took t his tragedy to get the Government to
actually take action. And yes, it did some things, but as time has gone on, as Pike River
has become more and more of a distant memory, and, as we get close to the 5- year
4724 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 24 Jun 2015
anniversary of that tragic day, it has become so mething that has slipped slowly off the
National Party’s political radar.
It is out of frustration for the fact that that has happened that my colleague Damien
O’Connor has introduced this legislation and left it on the Order Paper, even though it
has been sitting on the Order Paper for some time because of the National Party’s
filibustering of a range of members’ bills on members’ day. It has remained on the
Order Paper because it is still relevant. In fact, it is more relevant now, with the
National Part y divided over health and safety, than it was a month ago. The National
Party now is not sure if it wants to water down the health and safety reforms that it is
introducing or beef them up with corporate manslaughter. It has no idea what it is doing
on this. It is getting pulled in all directions by all its different corporate interests —by
Talley’s, which want there to be no health and safety legislation at all in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: And they’ve got the money.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: And they have got the money, too. That is why: out of
frustration that the Government has failed to actually finish the job and make sure that
not only our underground coal mines are safe, but our quarries are safe, our forests are
safe, our farms are safe, and our fishing vessels are safe— all those industries that are
killing and maiming New Zealanders. We should still be focused like a laser on
addressing those issues. But it is no longer a focus for this Government.
We are still waiting to see what it is that the Government wants to do, since it has
delayed the health and safety legislation. We have no idea what it is that the
Government actually plans to do with that legislation. I think it has no idea what it plans
to do with that legislation. All it knows is it is not in its DNA to make workplaces safer.

items.speaker: So I say to the Government members
items.text: demonstrate to the people of New Zealand that it
is in your DNA, that it is something that you are committed to, and that it is something
you are focused on by supporting this legislation in the name of the Hon Damien
O’Connor. Do not forget Pike River—do not forget Pike River. Finish the job and make
not only our mines safer but every workplace in New Zealand safer.

items.speaker: ALASTAIR SCOTT
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity. First
of all, I would like to commend Mr O’Connor for his initiative in bringing this bill to
the House, his motivation for bringing this bill to  the House, and, last but not least, his
obvious action, because actions are what matter.
This bill was brought to the House as a result of the Pike River disaster, but I would
like to also acknowledge that it is part of a concerted effort that is going o n in health
and safety, not just in this House but in industries across the country. The Government
is aiming to reduce deaths by 25 percent by 2020. Some of those initiatives include the
maritime operator safety system, the “MOSS” regulations, which have been in for about
12 months. The forestry sector is collaborating together to increase the health and safety
of its workers. FarmSafe is working with Federated Farmers, who are working with
WorkSafe and are engaged in a whole lot of initiatives to make sur e that their workers
are safe. The previous speaker suggested that this party is not concerned about the
safety of workers in this country. That is just totally rejected. That is why we have
introduced the Health and Safety Reform Bill, which has, as has a lready been
mentioned, superseded this member’s bill.
I agree with Mr Lees -Galloway. The statistics in this country are not good—75
deaths per year is not a good record. About 40 percent or, let us just put it another way,
about 29 people die in the agric ulture sector alone every year —the same number of
people who died in the Pike River disaster. That is every year. That is just every year,
and that has got to be considered. There are going to be thousands of injuries, let alone
the deaths, and thousands of families who are affected by slack, poor health and safety
regulations and practices that have been in this country for too long.
24 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4725
As a result of the Pike River inquiry there are 16 recommendations. I can tell the
House that they have all been considered and implemented, including consideration of
the Australian mining regulations, which are the basis of this member’s bill. As I say,
because the Health and Safety Reform Bill has superseded the member’s bill, I cannot
support Mr O’Connor’s bill. But it is not just about the paperwork. It is not just about
the bill; it is about attitude and culture, which are the key drivers to having a safe
environment. “She’ll be right” when it comes to health and safety is not right. A bit of
No. 8 wire is not good enough when it comes to the health and safety of our colleagues
and workmates. This cultural change that will take place will take time.
I would like to acknowledge at this point the previous chief executive officer of
Transpower from 2007 to 2014, Dr Patrick Str ange, who, at the top of his agenda at
every board meeting, had as an agenda item not the financials and the number of
kilometres of cable that had been strung up but the health and safety record of the
Transpower board over the previous month. He has led the way since before I was on
that board, and he is an example of leadership in the field of health and safety.
We need to continue to lead from the front. Just think about 20 years ago when we
talked about drink-driving culture. The laws were put in plac e, but we know my parents
and my grandparents continued to drink and drive. How long did seatbelts take to get in
place? That took years. I recall my parents not putting their seatbelt on, despite the law,
and my old man was a cop. So it is about a change in culture and attitude that must take
place; it is not just going to be about the legislation. But we will persist and we must
persist in developing the health and safety legal framework, and we must get it right. To
Mr Lees-Galloway’s point—we must get it right and a couple of weeks will not hurt. It
is important for the benefit of all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: I attended most days of the hearings of the Royal
Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy. It was unusual for the
commissioners themselves to ask many questions, but one of the ones that really sticks
in my mind was a question asked by Stewart Bell , one of the commissioners. In his day
job he is the Commissioner for Mine Safety and Health Queensland. He asked Doug
White, who is one of the managers from Pike River and an extremely experienced
coalminer, whether in his experience he had ever encounter ed a situation where the
regulator had made no notices to the mining company for any changes or improvements
in health and safety. Doug White answered no. Commissioner Bell was clearly aghast at
the gulf that existed between Queensland mine safety regulati ons and those that
pertained in New Zealand.
That gulf came from decades of Governments that either had actively shrunk the
State and the role of the State, or had not done enough to pull that role back and reverse
those changes. The two particular axe blows to mine-worker safety came in the 1990s at
the hands, particularly, of Bill Birch and Max Bradford when they gutted mine safety
regulations and then eliminated the role of check inspectors and largely dismantled the
Government’s mine inspection service as well.
I live close to the Pike River coalmine site. Many of those affected directly by the
tragedy were my friends and neighbours. I am proud of the role I played in forcing the
Government from its initial position of stonewalling and a Bart Simpson “ Nothing to
see here” attitude into, instead, first creating the High Hazards Unit and then Worksafe
New Zealand, and overhauling mine safety regulations, and then overhauling workplace
health and safety legislation. Those have all been good developments.
The question is whether or not enough has been done. The picture I certainly have is
of a Government that is very much in two minds. I think Iain Lees -Galloway is right
that one of those minds was forced by the circumstances that immediately followed the
Pike River disaster. I do not believe that any of those changes that the Government has
4726 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 24 Jun 2015
made have gone as far as I would take them. On the next day after the publication of the
royal commission’s report, I asked the Prime Minister whether he accepted that
deregulation had been a primary cause of the disaster. He did not. He did not accept it.
When we considered the first of the Government’s health and safety bills, we had the
quarrying industry submitting that it should be exempted from some of the measures
that pertained to mining and quarrying, and it won. The Government allowed the
industry to be exempted from those provisions, with tragic consequences.
I am certainly reminded of a question that I asked a former Minister, Kate Wilkinson,
on a number of occasions. I asked her whether on the day before the Pike River disaster
she would have said that the Government had done all it could to ensure the safety of
miners going to work that day. It was a very difficult question for her to answer because
there is always something we can do. So what I ask in relation to this bill is what can
possibly be wrong with our allowing this bill to go forward to a select committee to
enable members of the public, mine workers, and the companies themselves to tell us
whether enough has been done? What can be more important for us in this House than
to ensure that mine workers go to work each day and then come home?

items.speaker: ANDREW BAYLY
items.text: No one can doubt the  genuine intention
behind this Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill that is before us today. Each of us
clearly remembers the tragedy at Pike River, the enormous national wave of feeling and
reaction, and, later on, the deliberations and the debate of the royal commission.
This Government has acted on all of the recommendations of the royal commission.
One of these recommendations specified or requested the urgent establishment of an
“effective regulatory framework for underground coal mining”. At that time  reference
was made to the Queensland and also the New South Wales mining industries as
demonstrating best practice. As a result, this Government has worked with those areas
and the experts from those areas and also with our own coalmining industry in orde r to
improve and develop our own safety regulations to ensure that a disaster like Pike River
cannot or should not happen again.
Following on from this, in late 2013 Parliament passed legislation to significantly
improve work safety in this country and included specific new regulations to address the
coalmining industry. There were six principle provisions that were put forward through
that legislation. The first one was about putting in place health and safety management
systems. The second one was about appointing people to the newly created High
Hazards Unit, part of WorkSafe New Zealand. I note that 17 of those High Hazards Unit
inspectors have already been appointed and are in place. The third one was about
ensuring workers meet new competency requirem ents; the fourth about complying with
strengthened emergency standards and, related to that, making sure that we had the right
emergency preparedness; and, finally, the fifth was about having notification and
reporting requirements that were suitable and appropriate. WorkSafe New Zealand has
been established and its funding has been recently boosted by $30 million. The High
Hazards Unit, as I mentioned before, is already in operation.
I also note that the Government has made changes to the Electricity (Saf ety)
Regulations 2010 to complement the new mining regulations. Three new changes were
made. The first one was about ensuring the competency of those carrying out electrical
work in mining operations is appropriate, the second was about improving the desig n
requirements, assessments, and verification of safety for mining equipment, and the last
was about regulating and endorsing the technical requirements and maintenance of
equipment used in mines. Other changes have been made to the Health and Safety in
Employment Act 1992. They have been specifically tailored to this industry. These
came into force in December 2013.
24 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4727
As a result of the Government’s wide -ranging reforms, New Zealand’s current
approach towards health and safety is nearing best practice. The Government has clearly
demonstrated its determination to continue the process towards making sure all workers
operating in the coalmining industry are safe and that we have in place the appropriate
safety practices. The reforms aim to reduce injury and death by 25 percent by the year
2020. WorkSafe New Zealand is one of the most significant overall reforms. It currently
carries out about 12,500 operational inspections each year.
The new Health and Safety Reform Bill is currently before the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee and has been subject to long and lengthy debate. We
have had the opportunity to hear many submissions. We are committed to getting it
right. It is a collaborative effort with all parties in Parliament. I do note that in schedule
2 of the original draft of the bill there is specific mention of an area dealing with the
mining industry. All these important initiatives have consequently pre -empted the
proposals of this bill and rendered its introduction redundant in view of the wide  scope
of changes and the overarching regulations that have already come into place.
Although commending the purpose of the Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill, this
National Government considers it to be a duplication of all the good work that has gone
on and is currently going on. As such, we do not support its introduction.

items.speaker: CLAYTON MITCHELL
items.text: I rise to take a short call for New Zealand
First on this very important matter, the Und erground Coal Mining Safety Bill,
introduced by the honourable member Damien O’Connor. I, unlike Jonathan Young,
will not hold out until the end of my speech to let you know where we stand as a party.
In fact, it was at the very last minute, in extra time,  that he told us where National was
going to go with it, and it was no surprise to us that, of course, National members do not
support it. New Zealand First wants to come out strongly, in the strongest of terms, to
say that we support this initiative by the honourable member Damien O’Connor.
I stand with pride, because if my grandfather was alive today he would be very much
appreciative that we have got the likes of the Labour Party and the Greens and New
Zealand First supporting this bill, because it is looking after the welfare of our workers.
My grandfather was the head of the miners’ union for some 20 years and was actually
present in 1967 when they had the Strongman Mine disaster where 19 men lost their
lives. Now we are coming up to 5 years this year since the death toll of 29 workers who
lost their lives at Pike River. This is the largest issue that we have got around the
country. This is a bigger issue than how much we are paying as a minimum wage for
our workers. Every single worker in this country has the right to absolutely be
guaranteed that they are going to go home after work. We as a country have got an
appalling record in terms of health and safety when we compare ourselves to the likes of
Australia, the United Kingdom, Germany, and the USA.
I asked to be on the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee, which many of
my friends across the House are a part of as well. We are right in the middle of
deliberations on the Health and Safety Reform Bill, and yet again time has been
extended even further. What we are trying to say here is that we have got a bill in place
that could be implemented rather quickly and under some sort of urgency to look after
the lives of those mine workers. It was only 10 days ago that another quarry worker was
killed. I know it was not an underground mining situation, but it just goes to show the
lackadaisical legislation we have got around health and safety in this country. Yes, after
Pike River the Government came out and said it wanted to do something about it. It said
it would act quickly and put some regulations in place and make sure that the death toll
comes down in this sector. What it did not do was actually fund health and safety
adequately to ensure that those regulations were actually managed and policed
4728 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 24 Jun 2015
adequately to ensure that those deaths stopped happening, and, of course, we are still
finding the same old story. We are going over and over it again.
I urge this Government to change its position of not supporting this bill. I would like
to say also that Damien O’Connor has been in Parliament for some 22 years, and for all
but 3 of those years he has held the seat of West Coast -  Tasman. He has held that seat
and he stands up and speaks for those people because he actually gets to see them and
speak to them on a regular basis. When he has to go and talk to his constituents from his
area and explain to them that he is doing everything he can, it is frustrating for him to
actually not be able to go back with something solid that is supported —not for any
political reasons but for good reasons—in this House.
I would just like to finish by saying that the coal mining industry makes up about 2.5
percent of our country’s GDP and about 6.2 percent of our total exports. But it actually
does more than that. For our r egions, particularly in the West Coast -  Tasman area, it
makes up about 40 percent of our GDP. It has high- quality workers who are well and
truly getting paid over and above the New Zealand average wage, and, of course, down
there the average wage is about  $105,000 a year. The industry provides about 8,000
jobs. If we do not do something to keep our workers safe, if we do not do something to
look after this industry for our regional and rural parts of the country, we are going to be
in a very dire situation in the future.
We are waiting with bated breath for the current legislation, the Health and Safety
Reform Bill, to go through, and we urge the members of the Government on the
benches opposite to support the Underground Coal Mining and Safety Bill in the  name
of the Hon Damien O’Connor. We commend this bill to the select committee. We hope
it gets support. It makes good sense for it to get support, and we wish it all the best in its
endeavours. We will never forget the tragedy of Pike River. We will never  forget the
tragedies of the Strongman Mine, Ralph’s Mine, and other disasters around the country.
Those memories will be etched in the minds of all those family members and New
Zealanders who were there and know people who lost their lives on those very sad days.
Thank you.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: I rise in opposition to the Underground
Coal Mining Safety Bill, but, as my colleagues have done, I will not move any further
without acknowledging the intention behind this bill. It is extremely admirable that the
member Damien O’Connor has brought this to the floor in response to a tragedy that
should not have happened, and that, of course, is the Pike River mine tragedy. We ar e
shortly coming up to the anniversary of that disaster where 29 men on the West Coast
lost their lives. I can certainly say as someone who comes from a tight -knit community
that when a tragedy such as that occurs, everybody would have known one, if not ma ny,
of those men, and my sympathies are with those families in that community, where such
a huge and significant tragedy has occurred. It was a tragedy that should never have
happened, but now we need to move forward and certainly learn from it. But as my
other colleagues have mentioned, time has moved on and events have superseded this
bill. Following on from Pike River, there was, of course, the royal commission into the
tragedy and there were 16 recommendations from its report. It should be noted that the
Government has adopted those recommendations, and one of those, of course, is to
reform our law in respect of health and safety, acknowledging that New Zealanders as a
culture require a step change in health and safety—a step change in how we view it, and
a step change in how we deal with health and safety in the workplace —and that is
certainly something that the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee has been
looking at over the past months.
I just want to pick up on a point raised by the member opposite —Mr Lees-Galloway.
He suggested that this side of the House is deliberately slowing down the legislation.
24 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4729
Well, yes, we are, because we want to get health and safety legislation right. This is the
biggest reform in 25 years, and we need to make sure  that the law is fit for purpose. We
have a new concept coming into play, a PCBU, or person conducting a business or
undertaking, and we must make sure that that is fit for purpose not only for our large,
high-risk industries but also for the businesses that are low risk. But in acknowledging
that in respect of Pike River, in 2013 new regulations were introduced in respect of
mining administration, and what they did was require mining operators to “put in place
new health and safety management systems; appo int people to new safety critical roles;
make sure their workers meet new competency requirements; comply with strengthened
minimum standards; meet new requirements for emergency preparedness … and; meet
notification and reporting requirements.” So that in itself is a step change, but this new
Government bill coming into play, a bill that will again raise the bar, means that New
Zealanders have to take health and safety seriously and look at it as an integral part of
their business. As part of that the Gove rnment has established WorkSafe New Zealand,
and the challenge will lie with it to get the balance between carrot and stick to
encourage businesses to look at their safety culture, but also to take a hard line on those
operators who are not compliant with health and safety laws and are not putting their
people first in respect of health and safety.
I just want to touch on some statistics. Obviously, it is part of the Government’s
programme to reduce deaths and injuries at work by 20 percent by 2020. If we l ook
across some of those high- risk sectors we can see that we definitely need a reduction —
for example, in the rural agriculture sector there were 20 deaths last year. So this
legislation is timely. I am not apologetic for slowing it down. We need to take a  look at
it. We need to take this law reform seriously. It is the biggest law reform in health and
safety in 25 years. But in respect of this bill from Damien O’Connor, it has been
superseded by events, and despite the intention we oppose the first reading.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise in support of this bill put
forward by my colleague the Hon Damien O’Conner. If only what the last speaker,
Sarah Dowie, said was true. If only events actually had made this an irrelevant debate
for this Parliament— I would be fine with that. I would be ecstatic about that, because
that would mean that workers in workplaces, particularly the most dangerous workplace
of New Zealand—mines—would be safe. But, sadly, that is not the case, and that is why
we are debating this very important bill. That Government opposite has not seen fit to
make this issue a priority, as it should be.
I recall speaking on one of the readings of the bill that the Government has  passed
with regard to mines safety, and I remember imploring this Government to never forget
what we have learnt from the Pike River mine and the tragedy that unfolded there. I
remember also saying to those members: “Please don’t do what I think this Parl iament
is guilty of doing in forgetting the Cave Creek tragedy and all the lessons that we learnt
from that particular series of tragic events.” It appears to me that the National
Government is going to go down that same path again. It forgot about what it  learnt
from the tragedy of not having strong enough regulations when it came to Cave Creek,
and it is about to do it again with regard to what the royal commission has told us about
the outcomes of the Pike River mine tragedy, and it is not even that very long ago.
As many speakers in this debate have said, on the West Coast, where my good
colleague Damien O’Connor is the MP and represents that area particularly well, it is
just as though it happened yesterday. It is just as though that tragic event happe ned
yesterday for the people of the West Coast, and the Government is already forgetting
the lessons. We know that it is forgetting the lessons, because it is holding up the Health
and Safety Reform Bill at the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee—it is really
clear that that is what is occurring. There is disagreement in the ranks of the National
4730 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 24 Jun 2015
Government. Members cannot seem to get their act together around this. The
Government is falling apart around this issue. Meanwhile the people of the West  Coast
wait. Meanwhile the people in workplaces up and down the land wait for the National
Party to try to get its act together so that we can ensure that workers return home safely
after they have been to work.
I agree with the person who spoke from New Zealand First, because, actually, this
issue does surpass what one gets paid at work. There is no point getting a great wage at
work if you cannot actually perform the function safely. If you are not going to make it
home to your family, there is no point in what the size of the pay cheque is. This issue
of health and safety should be paramount, and it should be at the forefront of that
Government’s thinking. It should be a priority for Government members, but what are
they doing? Instead, they are voting against this legislation, and they also watered down
the legislation that came from the royal commission where the commission said that the
legislation should have also have covered quarry workers. National watered that down,
and we saw the sorry consequenc es of that just a few weeks ago, and it is doing the
same thing with the Health and Safety Reform bill. It is attempting to water that piece of
legislation down.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How would you know?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, I would know  because I am on the select committee,
actually, Mr Bishop. That is how I would know. That Government is attempting to
water down the legislation, and that member will know this because he is in the
National Party caucus where they have been debating how they are going to water down
the recommendations from the royal commission. That is right. The recommendations
of the royal commission have become an item for debate in the National Party caucus
because those members cannot agree on whether they think worke rs’ health and safety,
particularly in the dangerous workplace of mines, should be paramount or not.
I just recently learnt that my husband’s great -grandfather, who was an MP for the
Ōhinemuri area, did several good pieces of legislation to ensure that the miners in that
community were made safe many, many decades ago. To me, it is an absolute travesty
that I am standing here debating the same issues that are still not addressed and, thanks
to that National Government, will continue not to be addressed.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
the Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill, which is in the name of Damien O’Connor.
The purpose of this bill is to, on an interim basis, bring in better protection and safety
for underground coalminers here in New Zealand by adopting Queensland’s regulatory
framework until we have a better process in place. I can see that this bill is inspired by
the Pike River mine traged y, so before I get into this bill I would like to say that my
heart and thoughts go out to the Pike River miners and their families. The whole
country—yes, the whole country —was mourning after those explosions. Everyone
expects to return home safely after their day at work. Health and safety is critical.
Health and safety at work is important. Employees and employers both know that health
and safety is important. Employers know that if they have a safe workplace, their
employees are happy, they feel safe, and they are more productive. There are fewer
interruptions, which leads to less cost to business, because all such interruptions always
lead to some kind of cost. Cost aside, in serious cases, it can lead to injury or even the
death of workers. No one can deny that workplace health and safety is important, but
things get overlooked and accidents do happen.
According to the type of industry, there may be sometimes some specific
requirements, measures, and practices that are required to be in place, and thes e
measures and practices should be able to address physical, psychological,
environmental, and other health and safety issues. Coalmining is a worldwide industry
24 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4731
and the way of mining depends on the geology of the coal deposit. Open- cast mining—
yes, it is economical but the coal seam should be close to the surface. Underground
coalmining is comparatively a very complex process. It is not as simple as just adopting
another country or region’s regulatory framework because it requires a good
understanding of l ocal coal deposits and technical and operational requirements. It
requires good strategic planning. It requires good risk management. Also we need
people who bring the right kind of expertise, because it is a very complex and hazardous
industry.
I can see the reason for this bill but this National Government has already done a lot
in that direction. This National Government has already fulfilled that commitment that it
made after that Pike River tragedy. This was in November 2010 when this National
Government initiated a royal commission of inquiry and then it was November 2012
when the royal commission made its report public. Then in December 2012 this
National Government released its plan to implement the key recommendations that were
made by the royal co mmission. For that, the Independent Taskforce on Workplace
Health and Safety was given the task of advising the Government on workplace health
and safety and also on the structure and form of a new independent regulator for
workplace health and safety. So this National Government has already developed an
effective framework for mining—all kinds of mining, not just underground coalmining.
I would like to actually list a few things that are already done. Legislation arising
from the Health and Safety (Pike R iver Implementation) Bill established a new
workplace health and safety agency —that is, WorkSafe New Zealand —and
implemented key recommendations of the royal commission. Three Acts were created
by the Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill: The WorkSafe New Zealand
Act 2013, the Health and Safety in Employment Amendment Act 2013, and the Mines
Rescue Act. So we can see that this National Government has already fulfilled its
commitment to the royal commission’s recommendations. I can see the reas on behind
this bill, but this bill is unnecessary because this National Government is already
investing significantly in health and safety. We know that working safer reforms in the
Health and Safety Reform Bill before the House are to reduce injuries and the death toll
by 25 percent by 2020. WorkSafe New Zealand is assessing 12,500 businesses every
year. We do not support this bill because this bill is completely unnecessary. This
National Government has already done a lot in that direction. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast -  Tasman): In reply, thank
you for the opportunity, and I appreciate those members who have contributed to this
bill, the Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill. This was my best attempt to react and to
take action from the report of the Royal Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine
Tragedy. It said, as one of its first things to do: “Major change required and fast”. I
drafted a bill. The only avenue available to me was through the member’s bill process,
and I put this bill in there. Unfortunately, it took some time to be pulled out. In the
meantime, I acknowledge that the Government took the recommendations and
developed changes to mining regulations and legislation, and then promised to move on
health and safety. There are 29 families who will remind each and every one of us of the
failings of Parliament and the failings of legislation to put in place proper protection for
their loved ones in underground coalmining.
About 2 months prior to the Pike River disaster, having written to the Minister of
Labour at the time warning her about conditions in the coalmining industry, I received a
reply: “I am advised by the Department of Labour that there is no recent change in the
pattern of mining serious harm notifications that might give cause for concern.” That
Minister has long gone, but what I have heard from the Government in this debate is the
same naive approach to health and safety and to min ing regulations that that Minister
had swallowed also. In the process of development of the legislation that has been
4732 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 24 Jun 2015
passed now for underground mine safety, the quarrying industry lobbied to be excluded,
even though it is acknowledged as being a high -risk industry, and now this Parliament
will be reminded by three other families who have lost loved ones in the short space of
time—in fact, in this year alone —in the quarrying sector that they wanted their loved
ones to return home from work as well, and the legislation and the absence of regulation
for quarrying meant that those workers were not protected. Scott Baldwin, Tane Hill -
Ormsby, and Murray Taylor have been killed in their workplaces because the National
Government was lobbied to make changes to the proposals from the Pike River disaster
and the recommendations from the royal commission, and it dumbed down that
legislation.
What I say in the House here is that the Government has made changes to
underground mining regulations and safety, and made some  improvements, but it has
also made compromises as well. What I ask through this legislation is that the
Government would support the bill going to a select committee to enable us to review
the progress that has been made and to ask the question of whether  we need to make
further changes. At the moment, the wider body of health and safety legislation has
been parked up because the Government is subject to lobbying. In the same way, there
may be families in the future who have every right to come to this Hou se and say “You
failed my partner. You failed my husband.” —not you, Mr Assistant Speaker, but this
House—because we ignored the wisdom before us and, through lobbying, dumbed
down legislation and did not have in place the proper protection for people at work.
This bill is a legitimate way of having a comprehensive review.
I acknowledge the Green Party and New Zealand First for their support —they too
see the wisdom —and I would like to acknowledge my West Coast colleague Kevin
Hague, who has always stood bes ide me in trying to force the Government into a better
space on health and safety legislation. The 1992 legislation and the regime were based
on a flawed philosophy, but this Government’s oversight is based on flawed
information, and so we face a situation where, because of lobbying and because of bad
information, this National Government is going to vote down this piece of legislation.
This is a lost opportunity that would have allowed us to review the progress that we
should be making in mining, quarrying, and workplace health and safety.
A party vote  was called for on the question, That the Underground Coal Mining
Safety Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 60
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 12; Māori Party 2.
Noes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.
ELECTORAL (ADJUSTMENT OF THRESHOLDS) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I move, That the
Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I
nominate the Justice and Electoral Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate
time I intend to move that the J ustice and Electoral Committee be instructed that as part
of its consideration of the Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill, it may
consider any amendment based upon the recommendations of the MMP review
conducted by the Electoral Commission in 2012.
24 Jun 2015 Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill 4733
This bill is the result of a long process that is worth recalling in order to give the bill
some context. It began with the announcement by the Government that it would hold a
referendum on whether or not New Zealand should continue to use MMP as our system
for electing our Parliament. As part of the legislation that enacted that referendum, it
was agreed by Parliament that should New Zealand vote in favour of retaining MMP, a
review would be carried out to consider some of the issues that members of Parliament
on all sides understood that the public had around MMP. In the event, it did come to
pass that New Zealanders did vote to retain MMP, but it was clear to us all that there
were issues with the system that the public wanted us to address. So t he review as
legislated for was carried out, and the review reported back to Parliament with a number
of recommendations.
The Minister of Justice referred the review to the leaders of all political parties
represented in Parliament at the time, asking for  their views on the recommendations of
the MMP review, and each political party responded to the Minister of Justice with their
views on each of those recommendations. At that point the Minister of Justice declared
that there was no consensus, and the proc ess stopped. It was in response to the fact that
the process was not going to be continued by the Government that my former colleague
the Hon Lianne Dalziel drafted this legislation. Upon her retirement from Parliament I
picked up the legislation, and shortly after I did that, it was drawn from the ballot.
The bill does three things. First, it abolishes the one-seat threshold that allows parties
that do not reach the party vote threshold to bring list MPs into Parliament; secondly, it
reduces the party vote threshold from 5 percent to 4 percent; and, thirdly, it allows for a
review of the party vote threshold after three elections with the new party vote threshold
in place. It is important that we consider why we need to implement these
recommendations from the MMP review. The one-seat threshold has never really served
any real purpose in the New Zealand context.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: It increases proportionality.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: I will address the point that Chris Bishop has
interjected on. The one-seat threshold was simply a carry-over from the German system.
In the German system there are a number of states. There are regional parties that must
reach a three-electorate threshold in order to bring list MPs into the federal Pa rliament,
and that has actually occurred only on four occasions since MMP was introduced to the
German system in 1949. The royal commission that recommended the shift to MMP
recommended the one -seat threshold in the context of abolishing the Māori seats. O f
course, Māori seats were never abolished, and therefore the one -seat threshold was
never required. I do accept the point made by Chris Bishop that a consequence of
retaining the one -seat threshold is that it can, in certain circumstances, increase
proportionality, but that was not the purpose for introducing the one -seat threshold. In
fact, it increases proportionality on an ad hoc basis. It increases proportionality only
when parties win one seat or more and when those parties gain enough party votes to
bring additional list MPs into Parliament. There are better ways of increasing
proportionality, and that includes reducing the party vote threshold from 5 percent to 4
percent.
Moreover, and most important in the public’s mind, is the fact that the one -seat
threshold, which serves no real purpose, has become something that has been abused by
political parties. What has occurred is political parties have made deals with parties that
may support them in Parliament, by essentially giving up a seat and encoura ging voters
to vote for the other political party, knowing that that political party will not reach the
party vote threshold but has an opportunity to bring MPs into Parliament through the
one-seat threshold. That is a situation that New Zealanders have re soundingly told us
they are sick of. It does not matter which parties do it—it does not matter which parties
4734 Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill 24 Jun 2015
do it—it is simply something that New Zealanders have loudly and clearly told us they
are sick of, and they want us as MPs to address this issue, w hether or not we in our
political parties stand to gain from it personally.
The other thing that this bill does is it reduces the party vote threshold from 5 percent
to 4 percent. That is an acknowledgement of the fact that getting rid of the one -seat
threshold does have an impact, in certain circumstances, on proportionality. In fact,
reducing the party vote threshold ensures that proportionality is increased at every
election, and that there is a clear rule that everybody has to meet. Every party, if it
reaches the 4 percent threshold, has the right to bring list MPs into Parliament. That is
clear, and it affects everybody, and it is the case at every election. It is not an ad hoc
way of increasing proportionality —list MPs will be brought in only in the e vent that
parties win one seat and only in the event that those parties gain enough party votes to
bring additional MPs into the House.
I want to address some of the concerns that have been raised regarding this
legislation. First is that there is apparently no consensus. Well, in fact, there has been no
opportunity for political parties to reach consensus. We were given an opportunity to
provide our opening position, the position from which we would be prepared to
negotiate with other parties. But what we  were not given was the opportunity to carry
out that negotiation —the opportunity to reach consensus. Sending this bill to a select
committee is, in fact, that opportunity to reach that consensus. Secondly, the issue was
raised that not all the recommendations of the MMP review were contained in this bill. I
actually appreciate that concern that has been raised, and, as I began my contribution, it
is my intention, in the event that this bill passes first reading and is sent to the select
committee, to move an instruction to the select committee to consider all
recommendations of the MMP review. That then gives us the opportunity to consider
the recommendations as a package and reach consensus around them.
However, on the issue of consensus, I would say ther e is a very clear consensus, and
that is the consensus amongst the New Zealand public, the voters who put us here, the
people who have clearly said they want us to address this issue. In a UMR poll, 71
percent of those polled were in favour of abolishing t he one -seat threshold. Just 13
percent were against, and 16 percent were unsure. It is clear in the minds of New
Zealanders that the one -seat threshold —coat-tailing, as it has come to be known—is
unacceptable and the public no longer tolerates it. They want us as parliamentarians to
address this issue. So those who vote against this system will be seen in the public as
putting their own interests and their own party’s interests ahead of making an
amendment to our electoral system that makes it stronger, mor e robust, and more
closely aligned with the way New Zealanders want our electoral system to work. So I
do ask members of Parliament to put a strong and robust electoral system ahead of our
own interests. Send this bill to a select committee, let us conside r all the
recommendations of the MMP review, and let us craft an electoral system that New
Zealanders can have faith in.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I have to start my contribution in this House, first,

What she failed to acknowledge in her contribution—which seemed to focus solely on,

The second substantive point that she made in her contribution was the notion that

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: That would have been a reasonable way for us to have that

The member across the way starts raising the issue of building consensus around this

4738 Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill 24 Jun 2015
should have MMP as an e lectoral system. The problem is that when you have got

due respect, do we really believe that ACT is going to want to get rid of a provision that

to take a considered view, it is probably a bit of a stretch to ask him to go that far. I
would w elcome a counterview from the member, but, obviously, smaller parties that
have relied on the threshold before and the life raft position within this bill are probably
not going to want to support it.

items.text: Labour is doing what is in its best interest too.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Jami-Lee Ross says that Labour has some self -interest in this
bill. I welcome him to stand up and go through all of that self -interest. Ultimately, we
just want good electoral reform, to the point that Iain Lees -Galloway has written to
every member of this House and has said that for all of the other issues that were in the
MMP report by the Electoral Commission, let us debate every single one of them at

If there is a view that there is not consensus in Parliament, I can tell you that the one

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to be able to rise and
take a call on this bill. If  there was ever a bill that was an answer looking for a problem
it seems to me that this is it. Actually, I am surprised that the member who has brought
this forward, given his Midas touch history with members’ bills, actually has wasted the
opportunity on  such a bill. But there you go. I guess we have got to put anything
forward that we think may get somewhere.
There are three main parts of this legislation and I want to address each of them in
turn. The first one is the reduction of the threshold from 5 percent down to 4 percent. I
have got to say that neither in reading the background nor the introduction to the bill,
nor in any of the arguments that I have seen put forward today, have I heard any
plausible rationale for that. You could argue that 5 perc ent is, in fact, just a random
number to some degree and that there is not necessarily particular meaning attached to 5
percent; but neither is there any meaning to 4 percent. So if we are going to change it
from 5 percent to 4 percent, then why are we not  changing it to 3 percent? Or perhaps
the Conservatives might like 3.6 percent after last time? It has equal meaning to say 3.6
percent, 2 percent, 4 percent, 5 percent —to me there is nothing specific that really says
that we need to pick just another random number.
In fact, when we look at the other countries around the world that use a proportional
system there is a wide range of numbers that are used. Actually, the most common
number used is 5 percent, but they vary anything from 10 percent in Turkey down to
0.67 percent in the Netherlands. From my perspective until I hear a specific rationale
that says 4 percent is somehow more of a magic number than 5 percent and is one that is
convincing to me—and, yes, I have seen some arguments; what I am saying is that I am
not convinced by them—that is an important part of it.
24 Jun 2015 Electoral (Adjustment of Thresholds) Amendment Bill 4739
Arguably, Germany has got a very system operating. A lot of people talk about the
success of the German MMP system, and it uses 5 percent. Yes, its threshold is three
seats to our one seat in terms of the seat threshold perspective, but what you have got to
remember, of course, is that Germany has 631 seats in its Parliament. So
proportionately the three -seat threshold in Germany is far lower than the one -seat
threshold in the system we use in New Zealand.
When it comes to abolishing the one -seat threshold—coat -tailing, as others have
described it—initially I did have some sympathy for this. You know, when you look at
the 2008 example that has been used, at face value to some people it does s eem unfair
and at face value it could seem unfair. However, I think that unless you are going to do
away with thresholds altogether in terms of percentages, actually they are really
important. If a person from a party by winning their seat finds themselves  in Parliament
it seems absolutely ludicrous to me that other people from their party, if they have
achieved some level of proportionality above the one seat allocation, should not be
there. There is no justice in excluding them if the party is in Parliame nt. So I think there
is no reason that I can see to do away with that if it is about fairness, because whichever
way you cut the cake there is always going to be some argument against fairness. There
is no perfect system; we have just got to get the best system we can.
In fact, I have heard it argued plenty of times over the years when we have had
parties represented in Parliament that have not even actually managed to win any seats.
It seems a little bit weird to me that sometimes we have parties represen ted—yes, they
might have got 5 percent or 6 percent of the vote —but none of the people in their party
were able to win an electorate seat. Some people have said that perhaps we need to have
at least one seat plus whatever percentage you get. There are all sorts of permutations
that we could come up with, but I do not think that discussing this bill any further is
going to take us any further.
Finally, it says in this bill that we should review it every 3 years —to put that in
legislation.
